primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the fish most commonly symbolizes people (souls/converts) gathered into the kingdom of God through evangelism, encapsulated in Jesus' call to become 'fishers of men.' Closely intertwined with this, and often treated as the primary meaning in historical Christian tradition, is the fish as a symbol of Christ himself and of Christian identity, via the Greek word ICHTHYS (fish) used as an acronym for 'Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter' (Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior) — an early Christian confessional emblem. In exegesis of the biblical text itself, the 'souls caught for the kingdom' meaning is primary; in devotional/iconographic tradition, the Christ/ICHTHYS meaning is primary.
primary_basis: Matthew 4:18-19 ('Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men')
Luke 5:1-11 (miraculous catch; 'from now on you will catch men')
Matthew 13:47-50 (parable of the dragnet — the kingdom of heaven is like a net gathering fish of every kind)
John 21:1-14 (post-resurrection miraculous catch of 153 fish, often read as symbolizing the church's evangelistic mission)

alternatives.meaning: Fish as a symbol of Christ himself (ICHTHYS acrostic), used by early Christians as an identifying sign; grounded in patristic writers (e.g., Tertullian, Augustine) and catacomb art rather than a specific biblical proof-text.
basis: Tertullian, On Baptism 1 ('we, little fishes, after the image of our ICHTHYS Jesus Christ, are born in water')
Associated loosely with John 21:9-13 and the feeding miracles

alternatives.meaning: Fish as a symbol of the believer/Christian ('little fish' born in the waters of baptism), an extension of the ICHTHYS tradition emphasizing baptismal identity.
basis: Early Christian catacomb and baptistery iconography

alternatives.meaning: Fish as a sign of miraculous divine provision and God's care, drawn from the feeding miracles and related episodes.
basis: Matthew 14:13-21 and 15:32-39 (feeding of the 5,000 and 4,000 with loaves and fish)
Luke 24:42-43 and John 21:9-13 (the risen Christ eating/serving fish)

alternatives.meaning: Jonah's great fish as a type of Christ's death, burial, and resurrection (the 'sign of Jonah'). This is a well-recognized typology but concerns a specific narrative fish rather than fish as a general symbol.
Fish (with bread) as a Eucharistic symbol, based on the feeding miracles and John 21, prominent in early Christian art and some patristic and Catholic interpretation.
basis: John 6 (feeding miracle followed by the bread-of-life discourse)
Early Christian funerary art (e.g., catacomb banquet scenes)

alternatives.meaning: Good and bad fish in the dragnet as symbols of the righteous and the wicked at the final judgment (the fish stand for the mixed membership of the visible kingdom).
Fish/fishing as an image of judgment or capture of nations in prophetic literature (people 'caught' for judgment rather than salvation), noted in academic Old Testament interpretation.
Abundant fish in Ezekiel's river vision as a symbol of eschatological life, healing, and abundance flowing from God's temple.

notes: Fish is one of the most stable symbols in Christian tradition, but its consensus is twofold: (1) exegetically, fish represent people gathered for the kingdom ('fishers of men,' the dragnet, the miraculous catches); (2) traditionally/iconographically, the fish represents Christ via the ICHTHYS acrostic and, derivatively, the Christian believer. Both strands are extremely well attested and mutually reinforcing rather than competing. Secondary readings (provision, Eucharist, sign of Jonah, judgment imagery in the prophets) are recognized but context-specific. Assessment is given without knowledge of the author's thesis.
